verses.text: These are the words of King Lemuel—the burden that his mother taught him:
What shall I say, O my son? What, O son of my womb? What, O son of my vows?
Do not spend your strength on women or your vigor on those who ruin kings.
It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to crave strong drink,
lest they drink and forget what is decreed, depriving all the oppressed of justice.
Give strong drink to one who is perishing, and wine to the bitter in soul.
Let him drink and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.
Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed.
Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy.
A wife of noble character, who can find? She is far more precious than rubies.
The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value.
She brings him good and not harm all the days of her life.
She selects wool and flax and works with eager hands.
She is like the merchant ships, bringing her food from afar.
She rises while it is still night to provide food for her household and portions for her maidservants.
She appraises a field and buys it; from her earnings she plants a vineyard.
She girds herself with strength and shows that her arms are strong.
She sees that her gain is good, and her lamp is not extinguished at night.
She stretches out her hands to the distaff and grasps the spindle with her fingers.
She opens her arms to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.
When it snows, she has no fear for her household, for they are all clothed in scarlet.
She makes coverings for her bed; her clothing is fine linen and purple.
Her husband is known at the city gate, where he sits among the elders of the land.
She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchants.
Strength and honor are her clothing, and she can laugh at the days to come.
She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue.
She watches over the affairs of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.
Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband praises her as well:
"Many daughters have done noble things, but you surpass them all!"
Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates.

context.author: King Lemuel, passing on what his mother taught him (31:1-9), otherwise unknown. The poem of the noble wife (31:10-31) has no name on it.
context.genre: A royal instruction and an alphabet poem (acrostic)
context.audience: A young king (31:1-9), and every household (31:10-31)
context.setting: The book ends with two pieces about strong women. First, “the words of King Lemuel—the burden that his mother taught him” (v.1): she tells her son not to spend his strength on women or drink, because a king must not forget the law and must “open your mouth for those with no voice” and defend the poor and needy (vv.2-9). Then comes the poem of the noble wife (vv.10-31): “A wife of noble character, who can find? She is far more precious than rubies” (v.10). She works with wool and flax, buys a field, plants a vineyard, sells linen garments, reaches out to the poor, and laughs at the days to come (vv.13-25). “Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (v.30).
context.custom: The poem is an acrostic: its 22 verses begin with the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, from aleph to tav, as if to say everything from A to Z. Women spun thread with a distaff and spindle (v.19) and wove cloth at home, and good cloth was traded with merchants (v.24). Her husband “is known at the city gate, where he sits among the elders of the land” (v.23). In many Hebrew Bibles the book of Ruth comes right after Proverbs, and Boaz calls Ruth “a woman of noble character” (Ruth 3:11), the same words as v.10.
context.timelineImmediate: This is the end of Proverbs. In many Hebrew Bibles the next book is Ruth; in English Bibles it is Ecclesiastes, another book of wisdom.
context.timelineBible: The book began with the fear of the LORD as the beginning of knowledge (1:7) and ends with a woman who fears the LORD (v.30). Many readers see her as Lady Wisdom of chapters 1-9 lived out in a real home. Peter tells wives that true beauty is “the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit” (1 Peter 3:4).

translation.meaning: Strength, valor, worth, often used of warriors and of wealth. “A woman of valor.” The same phrase is used of Ruth.
The stick that held raw wool or flax for spinning, or perhaps a spinning tool.
Fearing, revering. The book ends where it began, with the fear of the LORD.

gospelParallels.note: True beauty is a gentle and quiet spirit.
Tabitha, full of good works, and the garments she made.
Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth.

otBackground.note: Boaz calls Ruth a woman of noble character.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.
The king must not multiply wives and must read the law.

overview.summary: King Lemuel’s mother teaches him to rule with justice for the poor, and an alphabet poem praises a strong wife who fears the LORD.
overview.settingLine: A queen mother teaches her son; a home full of wisdom.

history.t: Kings’ mothers had real influence (1 Kings 2:19).

customs.t: Wool and flax spun with distaff and spindle.
Verses start with each Hebrew letter in turn.

archaeology.t: Clay loom weights are found in many Israelite houses.
Small stone and bone whorls from spindles are common finds.

overview.discussion: The book ends with a woman who “fears the LORD” (v.30), the theme it began with in 1:7. What would it look like for the fear of the LORD to show up in the everyday work of my home?
overview.book: The book of Proverbs · 31 chapters. Short sayings and longer poems that teach how to live wisely in God’s world, beginning with the fear of the LORD.
overview.author: King Lemuel’s mother
